newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Mitterrand aide sees judge in bugging probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mitterrand aide sees judge in bugging probe.

text.p: A senior aide to late French president Francois Mitterrand went before a judge on Friday for the first time since vowing to spill the beans about illegal wiretapping.
Gilles Menage, former head of the Socialist president's private office, left the Paris law courts with his lawyer after four hours of questioning by investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat.

He is under investigation for allegedly authorising an anti-terrorism unit in Mitterrand's office to carry out widespread illegal wiretapping of journalists, lawyers and politicians from 1982 to 1986.

Menage told reporters he had promised to explain to the judge the reasons for the wiretapping of a first list of 15 people out of a total of 150 he is being investigated for, but would not disclose information that could endanger the security of the state or any specific people.

After vowing to answer questions fully about the tapping in order to defend himself, even if that meant violating state secrecy rules, Menage said in an interview published earlier on Friday he would not reveal secrets involving the 1986-1988 "cohabitation" period when conservative President Jacques Chirac was Mitterrand's prime minister.

"I am not here to weaken the state apparatus. The matters on which I am exempting myself from state secrecy rules, are strictly those which concern the current investigation," he told the daily France Soir.
"These do not concern events after 1986, when the first cohabitation began," he said.
Menage said he would not reveal the names of people who work for the government communications interception centre (GIC) which conducted the wiretaps.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe has reacted angrily to Menage's decision to breach state secrecy, which is punishable by up to seven years in jail and a 700,000 franc ($120,000) fine.
"I understand the prime minister's reasoning, but it is not the same reasoning as that of the justice system which does not accept being blocked by state secrecy," Menage said.
He said media reports had grossly exaggerated the number of people whose telephones were bugged, and said the anti-terrorist unit had wiretapped some 80 people annually.
The daily Liberation said some 100,000 people were illegal wiretapped each year.
In a television interview on Thursday, Menage singled out the prime minister's department and the defence ministry between 1983 and 1986 as the source of authorisations for the contested wiretapping.
Mitterrand, who was in power from 1981 to 1995, died last year of prostate cancer just eight months after leaving office.
